title: Public Universe: explore space and prepare an observing night
summary: Unreleased review draft for the first Public Universe community release. The proposed batch combines easier astronomy discovery with private observing workspaces, explained night-planning windows and clearer scientific provenance. Features described here remain in development pull requests; this is not a launch announcement.

Explore and learn: Explore, Observe, Learn and Data offer starting points for children, teachers, observers and researchers. Public catalogue browsing and learning remain free without an account.

Search solar-system objects and exoplanets together, with results from an available catalogue retained if the other is unavailable. Live searches keep the browser title aligned with the current query.

Browse measured planetary systems with ordinary name and distance filters, then open their planets or locate them on the galaxy map. The optional 3D display loads only when requested; its loading guidance changes when it is ready. Map redraw requests are combined when view changes arrive together; rendering does not run continuously while idle.

Learning activities explain stellar distances, discovery methods and measurements. Meteor-shower pages retain distinct observation campaigns and approximate seasonal guidance, not visibility forecasts.

Native filters, pagination, clearer keyboard focus and mobile navigation improve access. Orrery dates and partial positions, close-approach limits and small uncertainties have clearer validation and explanations.
Separate school and university resource pages connect free classroom handouts with printable undergraduate activities on orbital laws, exoplanet selection effects and reproducible data analysis.

The astronomy plugin guide explains setup for ChatGPT, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot and Claude, including the difference between a data connection and reusable skills. Public connection verification awaits the planned domain and Cloudflare changes.

A private feedback form lets visitors request features, report bugs or contact the team without an account. A reply email is optional; submissions go to the existing team inbox when mail delivery is configured.
Keep your own observing workspace: Save named telescopes, binoculars, eyepieces, Barlows, reducers, cameras and observing sites in your browser by default. Known measurements retain explicit units; unknown values remain unknown.
Sites can include a user-entered horizon profile. Import files are previewed before replacement, older workspace files remain supported, and imported sites are not silently activated.

Create observing lists and record actual observation times, outcomes and notes. Equipment and site snapshots preserve historical context after later profile changes. A planned target or list status is not proof of an observation. Correct a saved observation or rename a list without changing the target identity or historical setup.
Download JSON, CSV or print views with explicit location choices. Keep exports private: notes, dates and derived context can still reveal personal information even when coordinates are omitted.

An optional account copy requires explicit preview and consent to upload, restore or remove it. Signing in does not transfer your local records. Conflicts require a fresh choice rather than silent overwrite.

Account copies are encrypted by the server, not end-to-end encrypted. Removing an account copy leaves guest-browser data separate; local storage replacement still requires care when editing in several tabs.
Prepare a night, with its limits explain: Choose a date, time zone, rounded location and available hours, or explicitly copy a saved site. The night calculation applies your minimum altitude, supplied horizon, darkness and Moon-separation choices.

Request a small target shortlist for your chosen site, date and hours without knowing catalogue identifiers. Naked-eye, binocular and telescope choices explain how targets are ordered; optional field width and a source V-band magnitude cut remain your choices.

Shortlists cover the reviewed starter sample, Moon and planets, with calculated windows for suggested targets. Sampling can miss brief opportunities, so an empty shortlist does not mean there is nothing to observe. Equipment preferences and source brightness or size are not visibility guarantees.

Accessible charts and tables explain geometric windows for the Moon, planets and supported starter-catalogue targets. Empty, unresolved and unavailable results have distinct meanings. Newer calculations explain whether altitude and darkness requirements hold throughout, during part of, or during no resolved part of the selected interval; uncertain boundaries stay explicit.
Optional weather is requested separately for matching forecast hours. Missing or out-of-range forecasts stay unknown; clear weather does not establish that a target is observable.

Compare saved or temporary eyepieces by magnification, exit pupil and estimated field width, with field-stop values preferred when available. Camera previews use sensor geometry. These are geometric comparisons, not sky images or detection promises.
Equipment comparisons add sourced magnitude bands, quality flags and angular-size context to a plan. Unknown dimensions and historical double-star separations do not become invented target diameters.

Session downloads retain normalized inputs, windows, UTC times, time zone and method details. Coordinates and terrain are omitted by default and included only by explicit choice; CSV is a window index, while companion JSON carries fuller assumptions.

Seeing, sky brightness, optical quality, equipment compatibility and unmeasured obstacles can still prevent a useful view. This platform does not control telescopes or provide solar-observing instructions.
Read the source behind a result: A bounded starter catalogue brings sourced bright stars, overlapping historical multiple-star records and deep-sky objects into browsing and planning. It is not a complete sky survey; unsupported coordinates remain unavailable for calculation.
Coordinate frames, reference epochs, proper-motion assumptions and source-specific attribution remain visible. Unknown observation epochs or physical stellar distances are not filled with estimates.

Night calculations report their actual model, Earth-orientation data and, when configured, the checksum-pinned JPL kernel. Numerical boundary tolerance is not a statement of astronomical accuracy. Newer results also retain a reported algorithm-source identity; older omissions remain explicit.
Catalogue metadata distinguishes a logical data identity from a build identity and downloadable-file checksums. Older, changed or unavailable catalogues can have unknown identity.

The frontend observes catalogue identity to separate cache generations and compares API metadata with downloadable database metadata. An identity observed in a separate request does not certify that every result belongs to an immutable snapshot.

Filtered exoplanet-page downloads retain original measurements, units, limits, uncertainties and references. When the backend supplies identity read in the same transaction as those page rows, exports retain that association; older responses remain unassociated. This does not pin subsequent pages. Exact repetition still needs retained source snapshots, original inputs and compatible calculation software; a moving live API is not an archive.
Before this becomes a release: All changes in this draft are unreleased. The shortlist and refined constraint explanations have reviewed frontend and backend checkpoints. Combined local checks pass; remaining release and device acceptance is recorded separately. Reviewed topics and selected local checks do not mark the broader programme complete.

Local regression tests and selected browser checks do not establish field performance or physical-touch acceptance. Retained map measurements distinguish CPU submission time, GPU query time and resource counts; broader device and memory-byte measurements remain unverified.
The existing public addresses remain in use. The move to publicuniverse.net, live backend prerequisites, deployment and community announcement are separate decisions.
The permanent release page will be published only after the selected running version is verified. This draft does not change the application version or publish any notes.
